meta.regime: The regime is a physical energy supply shock running through a market where US real rates price everything else, and today it resolved into a single sentence: the dollar beat all seven peers while the war repriced only barrels. DXY is 99.615, up 0.50%, and every G10 currency lost to it - CHF -0.22%, CAD -0.35%, GBP -0.37%, EUR -0.52%, AUD -0.61%, JPY -0.71%, NZD -0.85%. Meanwhile WTI rose 3.72% to 103.773 and Brent 3.99% to 108.786 on a shut Saudi bypass pipeline and collapsed diplomacy, while GOLD FELL 1.74% and silver 2.19%. That combination - crude at a four-month high, bullion down nearly 2%, the franc soft - is the clearest statement available that this is not a risk-off market and that haven allocation is dead while the Fed is hiking. The second feature is that the commodity complex has split in two: energy is bid on supply, industrial metals are offered on demand, with copper down 2.87% today and 6.75% on the week. That split is now the main source of cross-rate edge on this board - long the energy exporter against the industrial exporter, short the energy importers. The third feature is calendar compression: the Fed, the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan all decide inside 61 hours, roughly 86% is priced on the Fed and near-certainty on the BoJ, so the tradeable content is guidance rather than levels - the dot plot, the MPC vote split, and whether the BoJ attaches a pause.

dailyRead: Two of this file's own calls were tested today and one of them failed, so start there. This morning JPY was held at +3 on an explicitly stated ground: on Friday, the hottest US core CPI day of the month, the yen still beat the dollar, USD/JPY closing -0.52% and the week -1.69%. That was the entire evidential basis for ranking Japan above the United States. It inverted inside one session. USD/JPY is 154.707, UP 0.71% on the day, and the weekly has flipped positive to +0.23%. The yen was the second-worst G10 currency of the session, and the cross-book confirms it rather than contradicting it: CHF/JPY rose, GBP/JPY rose, EUR/JPY rose, CAD/JPY rose, and only NZD/JPY fell - and that one only because the kiwi was worse still. A single 0.71% session would be noise; a 0.71% session in which seven of eight crosses move against the position is a cross-sectional signal, and the honest response is to cut. JPY GOES FROM +3 TO +2, level with the dollar. Note what this is not: it is not an argument that the Bank of Japan will not hike on Friday. TE carries consensus AND its own forecast at 1.25%, the September Reuters poll had 97% of 68 economists expecting it, DBS calls it 'almost a done deal' with a hawkish 25bp the most likely outcome, and 1.25% would be the highest policy rate since roughly September 1995. The cut says something narrower and more useful: with USD and JPY both at +2, USD/JPY is no longer a short, it is a RANGE into the single most concentrated 61 hours of event risk on the calendar, and every remaining yen short must now earn its place on the weakness of the OTHER leg rather than on yen strength. That is why NZD/JPY stays HIGH and everything else in the yen book is downgraded. Second, Canada's CPI released at 12:30Z and it corrected my 8am call within four hours. Headline came in at 3.0% y/y, exactly in line. But the MONTHLY rate printed -0.1% against a 0.0% forecast and +0.5% previously, core rose to 2.4% y/y from 2.3%, trimmed-mean held at 1.9% and median at 2.0%. This morning's file named the precise invalidation - 'a monthly print below 0.0% with trimmed-mean under 1.9%' - and exactly half of it was met: the monthly undershot, the trimmed-mean did not. So CAD is not cut, but the upgrade case is withdrawn, and the broader claim needs correcting. I wrote this morning that the petro-currency link 'came back'. The accurate version is that it transmits RELATIVELY and not ABSOLUTELY. USD/CAD is 1.39214, UP 0.35%, on a day Brent rose 3.99% to 108.786 - so oil did not save the Canadian dollar in outright terms. What it did do is keep CAD ahead of its peers: -0.35% against the dollar versus AUD at -0.61% and NZD at -0.85%. A frozen central bank with a negative monthly CPI print cannot beat a dollar carrying an 86%-priced hike, no matter what crude does; it can only beat the other commodity currencies. That is a narrower claim than this morning's and it is the one the tape supports, so EUR/CAD, AUD/CAD and NZD/CAD survive as cross trades while USD/CAD flips from RANGE to a LOW-MED LONG. Third, the haven failure that this file cut CHF on yesterday is no longer marginal, it is emphatic. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline - Petroline, 1,200 kilometres to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, carrying roughly 5 million barrels a day of crude that would otherwise transit the Gulf - remains shut after drone strikes launched from Iraq on September 10 and 11, with traders telling Reuters that Yanbu stocks cover only five to seven days of exports before as much as 4% of global supply is exposed. Late Sunday, Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi announced that Monday's Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting had been postponed 'in the interests of consensus' with no new date, hours after a vessel was struck near Qeshm Island killing one and injuring four. Crude priced it properly: WTI +3.72% to 103.773, Brent +3.99% to 108.786, EU gas +4.97% to 83.47 euros. And GOLD FELL 1.74% to 4274.88, silver fell 2.19% to 62.861, and USD/CHF rose another 0.22% to 0.81832. Bullion down nearly 2% with crude at a four-month high is as clean a proof as this market will give that haven demand is not being allocated while the Fed is hiking. Both XAU and XAG shorts are working for the stated reason, and the CHF crosses stay long. Fourth, the industrial side is now the fastest-deteriorating thing on the board and it has a date attached. Copper is 6.2839 USD per pound, down 2.87% today and 6.75% on the WEEK, against the -1.42% monthly figure that framed Thursday's discussion. XCU moves from RANGE to SHORT. And a correction to this morning's AUD reasoning, which claimed the domestic employment half of the two-part trigger 'cannot be tested until the September labour force report in mid-October': TE's calendar shows Australia's AUGUST labour force report on THURSDAY SEPTEMBER 24 at 01:30Z, with employment expected at +15.1K after -15.8K and unemployment at 4.5%. The employment half is testable in ten days, not four weeks. AUD therefore holds +1 today with two live tripwires rather than one - China industrial production and retail sales tomorrow at 05:00Z with consensus 4.8% and 0.8%, and the Australian jobs report on the 24th - and a miss on either alongside copper at these levels cuts Australia to zero. Fifth, the base rates, re-verified on TradingEconomics this morning and unchanged: US policy rate 3.75% upper bound with CPI 3.4%; euro-area deposit facility confirmed at 2.50% after the September 10 hike from 2.25%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90%, HICP 3.3%; UK Bank Rate 3.75% with CPI 2.9%; Japan 1.00% with CPI 1.9%; Australia 4.35% with CPI 3.5%; New Zealand 2.75% with CPI 4.1%; Canada 2.25% with CPI 3.0%; Switzerland 0.00% with CPI 0.8%. TE also now publishes the Fed's own projection rows - 3.8% current, 3.6% first year, 3.4% second, 3.1% third, 3.1% longer-run - which is the easing path Wednesday's dot plot either confirms or breaks. Sixth, the two currencies with nothing to report today are the two with everything to report tomorrow. Sterling holds at zero with GBP/USD at 1.34753, down 0.37%, into a 48-hour window that loads both tails: Tuesday 06:00Z brings unemployment expected to rise to 5.0%, average earnings including bonus expected to fall to 3.9% from 4.1%, and a claimant count where the +8,300 consensus is contradicted by TE's own -5,000 forecast; Wednesday 06:00Z brings CPI expected to rise to 3.1% with core at 2.7%. The euro holds +1 at 1.15383, down 0.52%, fully paid for a hawkish ECB and now carrying the board's largest energy-import bill with EU gas up 35.15% on the month. So the book into tomorrow: run the dollar longs against the commodity bloc, keep USD/CHF as the cleanest single expression, hold NZD/USD and NZD/JPY as the short legs, keep USOIL long against a shut pipeline while shorting the metals and the energy importers, and stand flat USD/JPY until Friday resolves it.

That narrower claim is what the tape supports, so EUR/CAD, AUD/CAD and NZD/CAD stay as cross trades while USD/CAD becomes a LOW-MED LONG rather than a RANGE. Wednesday's Summary of Deliberations at 17:30Z is the next signal.

CHF.when: Sept 24, 07:30Z - TE carries a 0% consensus and a 0% forecast
CHF.note: TE re-verified: SNB policy rate 0.00%, CPI 0.8% y/y with +0.4% m/m, unemployment 3.0%, GDP +1.5% q/q and 2.3% annual, manufacturing PMI 57.1 from 53.2, business confidence 107 from 104, current account 7.1% of GDP. The June SNB frame still governs: rate at 0%, medium-term inflation pressures largely unchanged despite energy-driven increases, Middle East tensions named as a risk that could STRENGTHEN the franc, and a signalled greater readiness to intervene. What would invalidate: an intact easing path in the dots is the sell-the-fact scenario and hits DXY, USD/CHF, XAU and XAG shorts together; lifting the out-year dots to flat or higher takes USD to +3 and re-rates every dollar pair.

What would invalidate downward: a hike Friday with an explicit pause attached, or a soft August CPI at 23:30Z Thursday against the 2.1% consensus, either of which takes JPY to +1. The reason is that the euro area is the largest net energy importer on this board, so the same supply shock that lifts Brent to 108.786 taxes European industry directly: EU gas 83.47 euros up 35.15% on the month, German gas up 29.32%, and euro-area July industrial production expected at -0.4% m/m on Wednesday. Policy tightening is priced; the terms-of-trade drag is not. That asymmetry is why EUR/CAD and GER40 stay SHORT. What would invalidate downward: any of this week's very heavy speaker flow - Schnabel, Cipollone, Lagarde and Machado today alone, then Buch, Vujčić, Elderson and Lane - softening the further-tightening language, or Wednesday's Q2 wage growth undershooting 3.4%. That is what a genuine weakest-link currency looks like. Consumer confidence collapsing more than fourteen points in a month is the market pricing that paragraph. Today's escalation makes it strictly worse rather than better: Brent at 108.786 with the Saudi bypass shut raises the imported-fuel bill of a small, distant, energy-importing economy whose central bank has already committed to looking through exactly that shock. With TE carrying a hold for October 28 there is no hawkish repricing available for six weeks. What would invalidate: a Q3 CPI showing core rather than fuel behind the 4.1%, forcing the RBNZ to abandon the look-through.

geopolitics: Two doors closed over the weekend and the market repriced exactly one channel. First, Saudi Arabia's East-West Crude Oil Pipeline - Petroline, 1,200 kilometres from the Eastern Province to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, carrying roughly 5 million barrels a day of crude that would otherwise transit the Gulf - was struck by drones launched from Iraqi territory on September 10 and 11 and remains shut as a precaution. Riyadh issued its strongest condemnation but said it would not retaliate for now, at Baghdad's request. Traders told Reuters that stored volumes at Yanbu cover exports for only five to seven days; past that window as much as 4% of global supply is exposed. This matters more than another tanker strike because Petroline IS the bypass - the physical answer to a closed Hormuz - and with it offline there is no workaround left. Second, late on September 13 Omani Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi announced that Monday's Gulf Cooperation Council-Iran meeting on the Hormuz shipping proposal had been postponed 'in the interests of consensus', at the request of unnamed regional states and by joint Tehran-Muscat decision, with no new date set. The postponement came hours after an attack near Qeshm Island, about 22km from Bandar Abbas, killed one and wounded four aboard an Iranian commercial vessel; UKMTO separately reported a vessel hit by a projectile with a severe fire and evacuation. Iran's president said 'Iran won't surrender'; Trump said Iran 'wants to make a deal so bad' that they are 'calling constantly', and when asked whether the US struck the vessel replied 'I don't want to say'. The underlying dispute is unchanged: Muscat's July proposal to split control of the strait 50-50 with voluntary transit fees was rejected by Tehran, which insists fees be compulsory and that it will not reopen the strait until the US naval blockade of Iranian ports is lifted. Hormuz traffic remains roughly 90% below pre-war levels against about 20 million barrels a day before February 28. Trump is pushing to restore flows ahead of November's midterms, which is simultaneously the strongest force for de-escalation on this board and the reason a sudden deal headline is a live tail risk against every position here. The FX transmission is unusually clean and unusually narrow, and today made it emphatic. Energy repriced hard: WTI +3.72% to 103.773, Brent +3.99% to 108.786, EU gas +4.97% to 83.47 euros with the monthly at +35.15%, German gas 80.65 at +29.32% monthly. Havens did the opposite: GOLD FELL 1.74% to 4274.88, silver fell 2.19% to 62.861, and USD/CHF ROSE 0.22% to 0.81832. Bullion down nearly 2% on a day crude hit a four-month high is the single most important read on this page - the war is being expressed exclusively through physical energy while US real rates own the haven bid, and no amount of escalation is changing that while the Fed hikes on Wednesday. The demand-side counterweight is what makes the crude rally fragile rather than structural: the IEA cut its 2026 global demand forecast to a DECLINE of 2.5 million barrels a day from 1.6 million in August, OPEC cut its demand-growth forecast for a fifth consecutive month and the EIA still projects Brent averaging near $90 in H2 on a gradual Hormuz recovery. Crude is rising on supply into a deteriorating demand picture, which means one headline - a pipeline restart or a rescheduled Muscat date - reverses it. IG's Tony Sycamore put the other side plainly: absent something operational from Oman, oil extends toward 119.48, the early-March high. Practically: hold USOIL LONG while the bypass is shut but treat it as headline-fragile; keep the CHF crosses long and XAU and XAG short, because three independent haven tests have now failed in three sessions; express Canada's energy advantage through the crosses - EUR/CAD, AUD/CAD, NZD/CAD - rather than against the dollar, since a frozen BoC cannot beat an 86%-priced Fed hike; and short the energy importers of this shock through GER40 and the kiwi.
